writing.explanation:
Send means a value may be moved to another thread; Sync means &T may be shared with one. They are inferred from a type's fields, which is why Rc is rejected at compile time while Arc is accepted — the difference is an atomic count, and the type system knows it.

`Send` allows ownership of a value to cross a thread boundary. `Sync` allows shared references to the value to be used from multiple threads; formally, `&T` is `Send` when `T` is `Sync`. These are marker traits, usually inferred from the fields of a type. A type may satisfy one but not the other. The distinction is about transfer versus shared access, so answer those as separate questions rather than saying a type is simply 'thread safe'.

`Rc<T>` is not suitable across threads because its reference count is non-atomic. `Arc<T>` uses an atomic reference count, so it can share ownership across threads when the contained `T` meets the required bounds. That does not make arbitrary mutation of `T` safe. If workers need to update one value, combine Arc with a mutex or use a narrower atomic operation. If they only read immutable data, Arc alone may suffice.

When the compiler rejects a value captured by `thread::spawn`, read whether the closure needs `Send`, whether a shared reference also needs `Sync`, and whether the captured value is owned or borrowed. Try moving a plain owned `String` first: transfer is fine. Then compare `Rc<String>` and `Arc<String>`. Do not add `unsafe impl Send` or `Sync` merely to satisfy a bound; those declarations promise safety to code you cannot inspect. The interview-quality answer gives both the trait definition and the design consequence.
